attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: 'We can certainly expect' is firm, unhedged expectation, so it is a scored forecast. The normalisation fairly captures further AI-related mistargeting incidents like Minab. No deadline was given.

contract.note: Requiring credible AI attribution is a fair reading, because Marcus separates 'this type' from ordinary targeting errors. The open horizon is correctly kept, and absence of an event is not treated as failure. One caveat: AI's role may never be disclosed, as Marcus himself notes.

evidence.note: Officials linked the Minab strike partly to over-reliance on Maven, but that strike happened on 28 Feb, before the post. It is not a further incident.
Covers the status of the Minab investigation in March 2026. It concerns the triggering incident only.
Concerns a 2024 Iraq strike, plus CENTCOM saying it cannot tell which strikes used AI. That predates the post and is not a later incident.

reviews.rationale: The forecast was firm but had no deadline. The packet has no credible report of an AI-attributed mistargeting with civilian deaths after 1 March 2026; the only AI attribution concerns Minab itself, which came before the post. The early-resolution rule is not met. Absence of such reports is not failure under an open horizon, so the forecast remains unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The 'unless and until' antecedent is kept. Adding 'in targeting' is a slight narrowing, but it fits the context. The claim is a conditional about a future state of knowledge and is essentially epistemic.

contract.note: The contract correctly treats this as not adjudicable. 'Really know' has no standard, and whether the antecedent was met (no military empirical studies) is undocumented.

evidence.note: CENTCOM says it cannot tell which strikes used AI. This shows how thin public knowledge is, but it cannot test the conditional.

reviews.rationale: This is a methodological, epistemic conditional with no measurable standard for 'really know' and no deadline. It is unknown whether the military has done such studies, so the antecedent is unknown and the conditional cannot be scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A present-tense, unhedged observation covering both reasoning and visual cognition. The normalisation is faithful.

contract.note: The plain reading (reproducible failures on tasks easy for humans, with benchmark progress not falsifying) is an ordinary reading of 'serious problems'. The target period chosen by the evaluator is reasonable.

evidence.note: Nguyen et al. v3 (Nov 2025): GPT-5 still falls far short on counterfactual visual counting. Supports the visual-cognition part.
Same paper: the newest tested models (GPT-5, Grok-4) show similarly poor, biased behaviour. Within the period.
Feb 2026 test: 42 of 53 models failed a one-step reasoning prompt. Supports the reasoning part. The publisher is a vendor.
Google's own claim of 77.1% on ARC-AGI-2 shows progress. Under the contract, benchmark progress does not falsify the claim, and this does not show the documented failures were gone.

reviews.rationale: In-period evidence shows reproducible failures on simple visual counting by then-recent frontier models, and widespread failure on a trivial one-step reasoning prompt in Feb 2026. Gemini 3.1 Pro's benchmark gain is a company claim of progress, which the contract says does not falsify the claim. Both parts hold.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: An unhedged present-tense observation. The normalisation is faithful.

contract.note: The plain reading (current mainstream models often fail simple common-sense questions) is ordinary and fair. The result does not depend on identifying the embedded example.

evidence.note: Feb 2026 test: only 5 of 53 models reliably answer the car-wash question, and 33 never do.
Reports the viral X thread of 13 Feb 2026, in which many mainstream models failed the same question. Within the period.
The human baseline was 71.5% correct and a few top models passed. This tempers, but does not negate, the finding.

reviews.rationale: Independent tests in Feb 2026 documented reproducible common-sense failures by most then-current mainstream models on a trivial question. Some top models passed and humans also erred at times, but generative AI as a whole clearly still had common-sense problems in the period.
